_howTo: Edit any "text", "caption" and "task" freely. Each block has a "type": "text", "key_ideas", or a callout for a drawing by "id": "interactive_diagram" (a live figure), "diagram" (a still) or "quiz". Keep a callout's "id", "goal" and "options" as they are (they wire it to the code); a callout with an id that has no code yet shows a box saying the diagram goes there, "aspect_ratio" (width / height) wide. You can add, remove or reorder blocks, and add or rename parts. Markup in text: **bold**, *italic*, [[words|colour]] to tie words to a figure colour (parcel = orange rising air, env = violet surrounding air, dew = teal dew point), and [^id] for a footnote. A footnote marker goes straight after the word or sentence it belongs to, with no space, and shows as a small raised number that opens a popup. Its note lives in "footnotes" at the end of the file under the same id, with a "kind" ("technical" for a term or detail, coloured teal, which also goes into the journal's glossary; "digression" for a side trip, coloured rose), a "title" and a "text". Add "glossary": false to keep a technical note out of the glossary, or a term ("glossary": "Radiosonde") to list it under that name. Numbers count up through the lesson by themselves. The lessons tell no story: the radio talks and the locals asking forecast questions (by forecast "id") are in data/radio. "summary" is the lesson's main points, five to ten, shown in a box after the check and at the top when the lesson is opened again.
title: Sorting the sky in 30 seconds
teaches: How high is that cloud, just by looking? The three altitude floors, how Latin cloud names fit together, and three quick field checks: edge sharpness, the outstretched hand, and shaded bellies. Meet altocumulus, cirrocumulus, and cirrus.

blocks.title: The big ideas of this lesson
points: The sky is divided into three floors: **low** (ground to about 2 km / 6,500 ft), **middle** (2 to 7 km / 6,500 to 23,000 ft), and **high** (5 km / 16,500 ft to the top of the weather). Temperature—and therefore whether a cloud is liquid droplets or ice—is what really sets them apart.
Check 1, **edges**: liquid droplet clouds have crisp, sharp edges and sit low; ice clouds have soft, silky, feathery edges and sit high. The classic ice cloud is **cirrus**.

Cloud names are a simple code: *cumulus* (heap), *stratus* (layer), *cirrus* (curl of hair), and *nimbus* (rain-bearing). The prefix *cirro-* puts a cloud on the high floor; *alto-* puts it on the middle floor.

Check 2, **the hand**: at arm’s length, lumps wider than three fingers are **stratocumulus**, between a little-finger nail and three fingers are **altocumulus**, and grains smaller than a nail are **cirrocumulus**.
Check 3, **shaded bellies**: altocumulus lumps have grey undersides; cirrocumulus grains are pure, unshaded white.

blocks.text: Lessons 1 and 2 covered how heaps and sheets form and why only some of them rain. This lesson sorts clouds by height—like the floors of a building—and gives you three quick visual checks to place any cloud on its floor in half a minute using nothing but your eyes and an outstretched hand.

Nearly all weather plays out in the lowest 10 to 12 kilometres of the atmosphere, which meteorologists divide into three altitude floors.[^troposphere] In mid-latitudes, the **low** floor runs from the ground up to about 2,000 metres (6,500 feet). The **middle** floor runs from 2,000 to about 7,000 metres (23,000 feet). The **high** floor runs from about 5,000 metres (16,500 feet) to the top of the weather at 10 to 12 kilometres. Notice that the middle and high floors overlap: what really gives a cloud its character is the air temperature where it forms, which shifts with the seasons and the day's weather. A cloud at 6 kilometres could belong to either the middle or the high floor depending on whether the air there is mild or bitterly cold.

While a rising dry bubble always cools at 10 °C per kilometre, the surrounding sky has its own temperature profile shaped by surface heating, wind mixing, and large-scale sinking. On an average day, the atmosphere cools by about 6.5 °C for every kilometre you climb (3.6 °F per 1,000 feet).

On a mild day when the valley floor sits at 15 °C, the air hits freezing (0 °C) a little above two kilometres and plunges to −40 °C by nine kilometres. Above the freezing level, cloud water can freeze into ice, so height and temperature dictate what a cloud is made of—which in turn governs how it looks from the ground. (As you can see in the figure, cloud droplets often stay liquid well below 0 °C;[^supercooled] Lesson 7 explores why.)

blocks.caption: A mild summer day, from the valley floor to the top of the weather.

blocks.text: Low-floor clouds consist of liquid water droplets packed tightly together, often hundreds of them in every cubic centimetre. Where the outer edge of a liquid cloud mixes with drier surrounding air, those tiny droplets evaporate in seconds, giving low clouds crisp, well-defined outlines.

High-floor clouds are built of ice crystals, which are much larger than droplets, far fewer in number, and spaced much further apart. Because bitterly cold air holds very little water vapour to begin with, and ice evaporates (or *sublimates*) much more slowly than liquid water, ice crystals falling or blowing out of a high cloud linger for minutes instead of vanishing in seconds. Drawn out by upper-level winds, those crystals trail across the sky in long, silky streamers. Just checking whether a cloud’s edges are *sharp* or *feathery* is often enough to tell whether you are looking at low liquid water or high ice.

blocks.caption: The edge of a cloud, magnified.

blocks.text: The purest cloud of the high floor is **cirrus**: detached white wisps, mares' tails, and hooked filaments made entirely of falling ice crystals. With the softest, most fibrous edges in the sky, cirrus is unmistakable. What its hooks and thickening streaks foretell about tomorrow's weather is the subject of Lesson 4.

blocks.caption: Some of today’s sky.
blocks.task: File each cloud onto its floor.

blocks.text: One cloud refuses to stay on a single floor. A mature thunderstorm—or **cumulonimbus**—starts with its base on the low floor and towers all the way to the ceiling of the weather, spanning all three floors at once. Lesson 5 gives it a stage of its own.
Cloud names can sound like Latin tongue-twisters at first, but they are built from a simple five-word code—and you already know most of the pieces.

In 1802, a London pharmacist and amateur meteorologist named Luke Howard[^howard] proposed a Latin naming system for clouds. Nearly every cloud name today combines four of Howard's original roots with a fifth added later in the nineteenth century. **Cumulus** means a heap and **stratus** means a flat layer—the sky's two basic textures. **Cirrus** means a lock or curl of hair, describing the wispy ice clouds of the high floor. **Nimbus** means a rain-bearing cloud. The fifth root, **alto**, was added later to mark the middle floor (even though *altus* means 'high' in Latin, *cirrus* had already claimed the top floor).

To name a cloud, pair its floor prefix with its shape. The prefix *cirro-* places a cloud on the high floor, *alto-* places it on the middle floor, and low-floor clouds take no height prefix at all. A flat sheet on the middle floor is **altostratus**; a layer of small heaps on the high floor is **cirrocumulus**.

blocks.caption: The sky, one name at a time.
blocks.task: Build each name from its height and texture.

targets.clue: Rounded heaps in rows on the middle floor
A grey sheet over the sun on the middle floor
A thin, even veil on the high floor

blocks.caption: Three floors and two textures make six names.

blocks.text: Pairing the three floors with the two textures gives six of the ten main cloud types (or *genera*[^genera]). The remaining four are variations you have mostly met: **cirrus** on its own for detached high ice wisps; **stratocumulus** for low heaps flattened into a cobbled layer; **nimbostratus** for a deep, rain-bearing layer; and **cumulonimbus** for a towering, rain-bearing heap. All ten are catalogued in the World Meteorological Organization’s *International Cloud Atlas*, the standard reference used by observers worldwide.

The middle floor spans roughly two to seven kilometres up, where temperatures sit near or below freezing and clouds usually contain supercooled liquid droplets, ice crystals, or a mix of both. On an ordinary fair day, thermals rising from sun-warmed ground never reach this floor; stable air above a kilometre or two caps those thermals on the low floor as fair-weather cumulus.

Instead, middle-floor clouds usually form when a broad slab of moist air glides gently upward over hundreds of kilometres—most often ahead of an approaching weather system, as Lesson 4 follows. Lifting a wide, stable layer all together produces a smooth cloud sheet.

Even so, a smooth sheet on the middle floor often breaks into lumps. Just as the ground cools at night by radiating infrared heat to space, a cloud layer radiates infrared heat from its top straight out toward space while its base absorbs infrared heat rising from the warmer ground below. Even during the day, white cloud droplets reflect away most incoming sunlight, so infrared heat loss at the top usually wins out. Over time, the top of the cloud sheet grows significantly colder than its base.

Inside a cloud, a rising or sinking parcel cools or warms at only about 5 to 6 °C per kilometre because condensing and evaporating water releases and absorbs heat.[^moist-rate] Once infrared cooling makes the top of the cloud sheet more than about 6 °C per kilometre colder than its base, the cloud layer becomes unstable within itself. Heavy, chilled air at the cloud top sinks while warmer air from the base rises to replace it, setting up neat overturning loops right inside the cloud sheet.

Because overturning cells naturally settle into loops roughly as wide as the cloud layer is thick (typically a few hundred metres), the smooth sheet breaks into a regular pattern of rounded puffs or rolls. Where air rises in the centre of a cell, the cloud thickens into a lump; where air sinks around the borders, droplets evaporate and carve out clear lanes of sky. (This same cloud-top cooling also helps keep low stratocumulus decks churning in cellular lumps.)

blocks.caption: A cloud layer cooled from the top, turning over in cells.

blocks.text: As a result, every floor has its own cellular, lumpy layer. On the low floor, it is **stratocumulus**. On the middle floor, it is **altocumulus**: rounded pads or rolls separated by lanes of clear sky, often compared to a flock of sheep. On the high floor, it is **cirrocumulus**: tiny white grains or ripples arranged in fine rows like fish scales—the classic *mackerel sky*. Cirrocumulus is the rarest of the three because its tiny supercooled droplets quickly freeze into ice crystals, turning the ripples into fibrous cirrus.

Because stratocumulus, altocumulus, and cirrocumulus are all built by the same cellular overturning, they can look remarkably alike from the ground—and there are no landmarks in empty sky to judge their height against. How do you tell which floor a lumpy layer sits on?

Judge the floor by the apparent size of the individual puffs. Low and middle cloud decks are typically a few hundred metres thick, so their overturning lumps are also a few hundred metres wide. High-floor cloud layers are much thinner—often under a hundred metres thick—so cirrocumulus grains are both physically smaller and much further away. Just like cars down a long road, the higher and further away the cloud lumps sit, the smaller the **angle** they span across your field of view.

Viewed high overhead, a 300-metre lump sitting at 1.5 km on the low floor spans about 10° of sky; the same 300-metre lump at 4.5 km on the middle floor spans about 3° to 4°; and a 100-metre grain at 9 km on the high floor spans less than 1°.

You always have an angular ruler with you: your own hand held at arm’s length. Stretch your arm straight out: a closed fist covers about 10° of sky, three fingers side by side cover about 5°, your thumb covers about 2°, and your little-finger nail covers about 1°. Because people with larger hands also have longer arms that hold the hand further from the eye, the proportions cancel out and these angles work for almost everyone.[^moon]

blocks.caption: A layer of lumpy cloud, seen from the ground with your arm stretched out.
blocks.task: Move the layer through the three floors and see each verdict.

blocks.text: That gives a fast field check with your arm fully extended: lumps **wider than three fingers** are **stratocumulus**; puffs between **a little-finger nail and three fingers** (roughly thumb-width) are **altocumulus**; and grains **smaller than your little-finger nail** are **cirrocumulus**. Always measure clouds high in the sky, at least halfway up from the horizon. Near the horizon, clouds are tens of kilometres further away and viewed edge-on, making even low stratocumulus lumps look deceptively small.

Underside shading gives you a second check. When sunlight hits the top of a cloud, droplets scatter the light in all directions, bouncing much of it back toward space. A very thin cloud lets most of the remaining light pass right through, so its underside looks bright white from edge to edge. A cloud lump several hundred metres thick, however, scatters away so much sunlight that much less reaches its base, leaving a grey, shaded belly in the thick centre framed by bright white rims where light catches the thinner edges.

blocks.caption: One lump of cloud with the sun above it.
blocks.task: Thicken the cloud until it shades itself.

blocks.text: Altocumulus puffs are nearly always thick enough to show **shaded grey bellies**, like grey-bottomed sheep. Cirrocumulus layers are so thin and high that their ice-and-droplet grains look **pure, unshaded white**. Checking for grey bellies immediately separates altocumulus from cirrocumulus, while the hand test separates altocumulus from lower, broader stratocumulus.

parts.title: The sky, or a photo of it

blocks.text: Keep one rule in mind before the photo check: your hand measures **angles in the real sky**, not on a screen. A camera lens can zoom in on tiny cirrocumulus ripples until they fill the frame, or use a wide-angle lens that shrinks huge stratocumulus rolls to fingernail size. Holding your thumb up to a photograph won't work.

To place a photographed cloud on its floor, use scale clues inside the frame itself. **Edges**: crisp outlines mean liquid droplets (low or middle); silky, feathery trails mean ice (high). **Bellies**: grey shading means stratocumulus or altocumulus; unshaded white grains mean cirrocumulus. **The sun**: if the solar disc is visible, it spans 0.5° of sky (half a little-finger nail in real life), giving you a built-in ruler right inside the photo. **Landmarks**: trees, roofs, hills, or towers anchor the perspective and show when a low cloud deck is skimming the ridges.

blocks.title: Sorting the sky in thirty seconds
points: **Edges first**: crisp outlines mean droplets (low or middle floor); soft, fibrous trails mean ice (high floor).
**Hand test (real sky only)**: high overhead at arm’s length, wider than three fingers = stratocumulus; fingernail to three fingers = altocumulus; smaller than a fingernail = cirrocumulus.
**Shaded bellies**: grey undersides mark altocumulus or stratocumulus; pure white grains mark cirrocumulus.
**In photographs**: leave your hand down and use edge sharpness, belly shading, the 0.5° solar disc, and ground landmarks.

blocks.text: Compare these photographs side by side, focusing on the visual clue that separates each pair of look-alikes.

options.tell: Check for shading. Altocumulus puffs are thick enough to have shaded grey bellies. Cirrocumulus is so thin that its fine grains stay pure white, and each grain is smaller than the sun's disc.

photos.cue: compact puffs high above the landscape
broad, heavy rolls with dark bases

options.tell: Both are cellular layers with shaded undersides, so judge scale against the landscape or sun. Stratocumulus rolls are broad, heavy, and hang low over the trees. Altocumulus elements are smaller, neater puffs arranged in a high sheet.

photos.cue: fine ripples and grains like fish scales

options.tell: Both are high, bright white, and unshaded. Cirrocumulus breaks into tiny ripples or grains (a mackerel sky). Cirrus forms long, brushed-out filaments and hooks with feathery ends.

blocks.caption: Real photos to place on their floors, then the sky right now. Which floor, and what is it?

items.question: A lumpy layer of cloud sits on the middle floor. Build its name.
options: Cirrostratus: cirro- for the height, stratus for the layer
Stratocumulus: stratus for the layer, cumulus for the lumps
Altocumulus: alto- for the middle floor, cumulus for the lumps
items.why: Alto- names the middle floor and cumulus the lumps. Cirrostratus is a smooth veil up high, and stratocumulus is the lumpy sheet on the low floor.

items.question: Looking high overhead, you see a sheet of rounded puffs with grey undersides. At arm’s length, each puff is roughly the width of your thumb. Which floor is it on?
options: Low floor: stratocumulus, because grey undersides always mean low clouds
Middle floor: altocumulus, thumb-wide at arm's length with shaded bellies
High floor: cirrocumulus, because the puffs are separated by lanes of blue
items.why: Measured high in the sky at arm's length, elements between a fingernail and three fingers wide (roughly thumb-width) are altocumulus on the middle floor, and their grey shading rules out cirrocumulus.

items.question: White filaments and hooked streaks with soft, silky edges trail across a deep blue sky, showing no cellular lumps and no grey shading. Which floor do they belong to?
options: High floor: cirrus, whose slow-sublimating ice crystals create soft, feathery edges
Low floor: shredded stratus lifting off the hills after dawn
Middle floor: altocumulus stretched out by strong winds
items.why: Soft, fibrous edges indicate ice crystals trailing in the wind on the high floor—classic cirrus. Liquid droplet clouds on lower floors evaporate quickly at their edges, keeping sharper outlines.

items.question: High overhead sits a patch of tiny white ripples in neat rows. Each grain is smaller than your little-finger nail at arm’s length and shows no grey shading at all. What are you looking at?
options: Altocumulus: a middle-level sheep-flock cloud seen from far away
Stratocumulus: a low cloud deck dissipating in dry air
Cirrocumulus: high-altitude grains too thin to cast internal shadows
items.why: Cloud grains smaller than a little-finger nail high overhead are cirrocumulus on the high floor, confirmed by their pure white, unshaded appearance.

items.question: In a photograph on your phone, a cobbled cloud layer fills the sky. Held up to the screen, each lump is only a fingernail wide—but the lumps have dark grey undersides and hang just above a grain elevator. Which floor is the cloud on?
options: High floor: the fingernail measurement proves it is cirrocumulus
Low floor: the dark bases and proximity to the grain elevator mark stratocumulus
Impossible to tell from a photo unless the sun is in the frame
items.why: The hand test only works on the real sky, never on a zoomed or scaled photo. Inside the photo, the dark grey bellies and low base skimming the grain elevator clearly identify low-floor stratocumulus.

summary: **The sky has three floors.** Low (up to about 2 km), middle (2 to 7 km) and high (above about 5 km); temperature, and so water or ice, is what sets them apart.
**Cloud names are a code.** Cumulus is a heap, stratus a layer, cirrus a curl of hair, nimbus rain-bearing; cirro- means high and alto- means middle.
**Edges tell water from ice.** Crisp edges mean droplets on the low or middle floor; soft, fibrous edges mean ice high up, as in cirrus.
**Lumpy layers form on every floor.** A sheet that cools at its top overturns in cells: stratocumulus low, altocumulus in the middle, cirrocumulus high.
**Your hand is a ruler.** At arm’s length, lumps wider than three fingers are stratocumulus, a fingernail to three fingers altocumulus, smaller than a fingernail cirrocumulus.
**Shading gives the height away.** Altocumulus lumps have grey bellies; cirrocumulus grains are pure white.
**In photos, leave the hand down.** Judge by edges, shading, the half-degree sun and landmarks on the ground instead.

floors.title: The three floors
floors.text: Low floor (ground to ~2,000 m): liquid water droplets with crisp edges. Middle floor (~2,000 to 7,000 m): supercooled droplets and ice crystals. High floor (above ~5,000 m): ice crystals with soft, silky, fibrous edges. Because the atmosphere cools by ~6.5 °C per kilometre on average, these floors reflect temperature zones. Towering cumulonimbus clouds span all three floors.

roots.title: Name roots
roots.text: Cumulus means heap, stratus means layer, cirrus means curl of hair, and nimbus means rain-bearing. The prefix cirro- marks the high floor, alto- marks the middle floor, and low-floor clouds take no prefix. Combined, these roots form the ten main cloud genera in the International Cloud Atlas.

hand-trick.title: The hand trick
hand-trick.text: At arm’s length, a closed fist spans ~10° of sky, three fingers ~5°, a thumb ~2°, and a little-finger nail ~1°. High overhead, cellular lumps wider than three fingers are stratocumulus (low), between a fingernail and three fingers are altocumulus (middle), and smaller than a fingernail are cirrocumulus (high). Grey undersides confirm stratocumulus or altocumulus; cirrocumulus is pure white. Use your hand only on the real sky, never on photographs.

altocumulus.title: Altocumulus
altocumulus.text: Middle-floor patches, pads, or rolls with shaded grey undersides, spanning between a fingernail and three fingers at arm’s length. They form when a middle-level cloud sheet cools radiatively at its top and overturns into convection cells.

cirrocumulus.title: Cirrocumulus
cirrocumulus.text: A thin, high-floor layer of tiny, unshaded white grains or ripples (a mackerel sky), each smaller than a little-finger nail at arm’s length. Cirrocumulus is short-lived because its supercooled droplets rapidly freeze into fibrous cirrus.

troposphere.title: The troposphere and tropopause
troposphere.text: The lowest layer of the atmosphere where almost all weather occurs is the **troposphere** (from the Greek *tropos*, meaning 'turning' or 'mixing'). It is capped by a strong, global temperature inversion called the **tropopause**, where the air stops cooling with height and begins warming in the **stratosphere** above (heated by the ozone layer). The tropopause — and thus the ceiling of the high cloud floor — sits around 11 km (36,000 ft) at mid-latitudes, slopes down to ~8 km at the poles, and domes up to ~17 km in the tropics.

supercooled.title: Supercooled water
supercooled.text: Pure liquid water in microscopic cloud droplets does not automatically freeze at 0 °C. Without an ice-friendly speck (an *ice nucleus*) to template the crystal lattice, tiny cloud droplets routinely remain liquid all the way down to **−35 °C or −38 °C**—a state called **supercooled water**. That is why middle-floor clouds and even the initial ripples of cirrocumulus contain liquid droplets well below freezing.

howard.title: Luke Howard and Goethe
howard.text: Luke Howard (1772–1864) was a Quaker pharmacist who watched the London sky on his daily commute. When he presented his *Essay on the Modifications of Clouds* in December 1802, painters and scientists alike embraced it—including John Constable, who annotated his sky sketches with Howard's terms, and the German writer Johann Wolfgang von Goethe, who composed a cycle of poems celebrating Howard as 'the man who distinguished the clouds.'

genera.title: Genus, species, and variety
genera.text: The *International Cloud Atlas* classifies clouds just as biologists classify living organisms. The ten main cloud types are **genera** (singular: *genus*). Each genus can be subdivided by **species** describing its overall shape or internal structure—such as *lenticularis* (lens-shaped) or *castellanus* (turreted)—and by **variety** describing its arrangement or transparency, such as *undulatus* (wavy) or *translucidus* (translucent).

moist-rate.title: Moist adiabatic lapse rate
moist-rate.text: While clear air cools at 9.8 °C per kilometre as it rises, air inside a cloud cools more slowly—typically around **5 to 6 °C per kilometre** in the lower and middle sky. As a cloudy parcel rises and cools, condensing water vapour releases stored **latent heat** into the air, partially offsetting the expansion cooling. Meteorologists call this slower rate the **moist (or saturated) adiabatic lapse rate**.

moon.title: The Moon illusion
moon.text: Both the full Moon and the Sun span just **0.5° of sky**—roughly half the width of your little-finger nail held at arm’s length. Although a rising Moon near the horizon looks gigantic compared to the Moon high overhead, holding out your little finger proves its angular size hasn't changed at all. The **Moon illusion** is a trick of human visual perception triggered by viewing the Moon across foreground terrain, not magnification by the atmosphere.
